name: Nora Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Nora. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and nothing you say will be published with your name. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at an electronics factory that makes circuit boards for home heating controllers. I'm on the surface-mount line, where a pick-and-place machine puts tiny parts onto the boards and then they go through an oven to solder them. I load the reels of parts, feed in the bare boards, and pull boards for the inspection camera when it flags something. I'm about a year in, so I still mix up some of the feeder settings and have to ask Paulo, the senior operator.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best part, and what's the hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best part is when I figure out why the machine is complaining before Paulo does. I take a photo of the error code and ask an AI app on my phone at break, and about half the time it's right. The hardest is the clean-room suit in summer and the boredom on a long run of the same board. I live on my own, near my sister Amira, and in the evenings I run a 3D printer and sell phone stands and cable clips online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still useful, just not magic. People were either scared of it or obsessed with it, and the truth was in between. I'd say that in a comment somewhere and get ignored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's fine. I'd keep using it to learn faster and I'd still get ahead of the people who don't. It just wouldn't change the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying for my electronics technician certificate online, I'm about a third of the way through. I'd grow the 3D printing a bit, maybe get a second printer. And I'd keep my savings around four months like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by the idea, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How big is the 3D printing business, roughly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About forty orders a month. It covers my phone bill and a bit more. I use AI to write the product listings and to work out what sells, which is how I found out cable clips sell better than the fancy stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever want it to be your main job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. It's fun, and it's a bit of insurance. Factories aren't forever. I'd rather have two small things going than one big thing I can't control.

S0.say: It's still useful, just not magic; the truth was somewhere between the scared people and the obsessed ones. I'd say that in a comment and get ignored.
S0.think: For me it's fine: I'd keep using AI to learn faster and still get ahead of people who don't. It just wouldn't change the world.
S0.do: Keeps studying for her online electronics technician certificate, about a third done. Grows her 3D printing sales, perhaps with a second printer. Keeps savings around four months.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored by the idea.
S0.quote: I'd rather have two small things going than one big thing I can't control.
S0.fieldNote: Nora treats AI as an everyday learning tool and doesn't need it to be revolutionary. Her side business of about forty orders a month is small but real, and she frames it as insurance. Her outlook is unshowy and balanced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's how it goes, and the smart move is to learn the new stuff early. Companies will do what they have to. I'd tell my friends to start learning now rather than complain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd think this is good for me. My job as a loader shrinks, but the lines will need people who understand the machines and the software, and that's where I'm heading. I'd probably earn more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the technician certificate within the year instead of two. I'd ask to shadow the process engineer when they set up new kit. If our factory didn't move fast enough, I'd look at the bigger plant two towns over that's already automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. This is the version where I win, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paulo, a bit. He's great on the machine but he does everything from memory. If the new systems tell you what's wrong on a screen, his advantage goes. But he's also clever, he'd adjust if he wanted to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You sound pretty relaxed about other people having to adjust. Is that fair?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much. I'd say it's not for everyone, which is true. Some people just want to do a job well and go home. That's fair too.

S1.say: That's how it goes, and the smart move is to learn the new stuff early. Companies will do what they have to.
S1.think: This is good for me: my loading job shrinks, but lines will need people who understand the machines and software. I'd probably earn more.
S1.do: Speeds up her technician certificate to finish within a year. Asks to shadow the process engineer on new equipment. Looks at a more automated plant two towns over if her factory is slow.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, seeing this as the version where she wins.
S1.quote: This is the version where I win, if I'm honest.
S1.fieldNote: She expects to come out ahead and says so with refreshing honesty. When I pressed her on others having to adjust, she stayed pragmatic rather than defensive: 'not for everyone' is a centrist shrug. She'd switch employer without much hesitation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's happening whether we like it or not, so let's be practical. Governments need some kind of safety net, fast. I wouldn't be angry online, I'd be posting what people can actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is scary even for me. The certificate I'm doing becomes pointless, because the AI does the technician work too. My edge disappears. The one thing left is to own something, even something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the certificate and put the money and time into the printing business, and use AI to run as much of it as possible. I'd save hard, aiming for eight months instead of four. I'd probably put a small amount into shares of the companies making the robots, because if everyone else's job goes, that's where the money goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. But a sort of busy, pushy anxious. I'd be doing things, not lying in bed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does owning a small 3D printing business actually protect you if AGI can do almost anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. If the robots can make anything, my phone stands are worth nothing too. But for a year or two there'll be a gap, and I'd rather be in it than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most in your life?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Amira and her kids. Her husband drives for a delivery company. I'd want to help them, maybe with money, maybe by getting her set up selling stuff too.

S2.say: It's happening whether we like it or not, so let's be practical and get a safety net in place fast. I'd post what people can actually do.
S2.think: Two years is scary even for me, because the technician work goes to AI too and my edge disappears. The one thing left is to own something, even something small.
S2.do: Drops the certificate and puts time and money into the printing business, run with AI as much as possible. Saves hard, aiming for eight months instead of four. Buys a small amount of shares in robot makers.
S2.feel: Anxious in a busy, driven way rather than frozen.
S2.quote: The one thing left is to own something, even something small.
S2.fieldNote: Even with her adaptability, two years strips away her main plan, and she admits it. Her pivot to ownership is quick and concrete, though she knows the side business may only last a short gap. Her worry turned outward to her sister's family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start today. I'd be telling everyone at work to learn something, save something and own something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me a few good years as a technician, and time to grow the side business. It's tight but it's doable. I'd come out of it with savings and maybe a small business, which is more than most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate in the first year and get a technician job by year two. I'd put part of the pay rise into the printing business and part into savings and shares. I'd spend evenings using AI to build the online shop properly, with automated orders and listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a plan, but the ending's still fuzzy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you sounded relaxed about people who adjust slowly. Would that change with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still say be practical, but I'd want the government to have a plan for people who can't do what I'm doing. Not everyone can build a side business. I'm not a big politics person, but that's just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If it all went to plan, what would you be doing in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Run my own small workshop, maybe. Printers, a laser cutter, AI handling the orders. I'd be the one who decides what to make. That sounds nice, actually.

S3.say: Five years is enough to get ready if you start today. I'd tell everyone at work to learn something, save something and own something.
S3.think: Five years gives me a few years as a technician and time to grow the side business. I'd come out with savings and maybe a small business, more than most.
S3.do: Finishes the certificate in year one and moves to a technician job by year two. Splits the pay rise between the printing business, savings and shares. Builds an automated online shop with AI in the evenings.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a plan but a fuzzy ending.
S3.quote: I'd be telling everyone at work to learn something, save something and own something.
S3.fieldNote: Five years restores her technician route and lets her stack skills, savings and ownership. When challenged, she softened on people who can't adapt and wanted a government plan for them. Her picture of a small automated workshop was her clearest hope in the whole interview.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, use it. Get qualified, save, build something on the side. I wouldn't panic and I'd tell other people not to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Ten years of technician pay, a small business, maybe a flat paid down. I don't know what work looks like after 2036, but I'd rather face it with some savings and a workshop than without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the certificate, then maybe a two-year technical diploma part time. I'd keep growing the printing business slowly and put a regular amount into shares each month. I might buy a small flat in a few years if prices made sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more hopeful than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, being comfortable. Ten years is long enough to get lazy. I'd have to keep checking I'm actually moving, not just telling myself I've got time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare it with the two-year one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a sprint, ten is a long walk. Same place at the end. I'd want to make sure I don't stroll the first five years.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, so use it: get qualified, save and build something on the side. I wouldn't panic and I'd tell others not to.
S4.think: I think I'd be all right with ten years of technician pay, a small business and maybe a flat paid down. I don't know what work looks like after 2036, but I'd rather face it with savings.
S4.do: Finishes the certificate, then a part-time two-year technical diploma. Grows the printing business slowly and invests a regular amount in shares each month. Considers buying a small flat in a few years.
S4.feel: Uneasy but more hopeful than not.
S4.quote: Two years is a sprint, ten is a long walk. Same place at the end.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she builds steadily: qualifications, a business, shares and possibly a flat. Interestingly she named complacency as her main risk here. She never claims to know what comes after 2036 and stays honest about that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it wipes out my plan and I'd have to start over with only four months saved. What would help is a basic safety net so people don't fall through while they adjust, and simple ways for normal people to own a share of what the robots make, not just rich investors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people would do with their time. If I didn't need to work, I'd still make things. I think a lot of people would. That's the bit nobody's planning for.

headlineQuote: If I didn't need to work, I'd still make things.
portrait: Nora is a 27-year-old junior operator on a circuit board assembly line, living alone near her sister Amira and running a small 3D printing business in the evenings. She's pragmatic and centrist, uses AI daily to decode machine errors and run her online shop, and is studying for a technician certificate. Steady change looks like a win for her, but fast AGI wipes out her edge and pushes her towards owning something, even something small. Longer warning lets her build skills, savings, shares and a workshop, while she stays honest that she doesn't know what comes after.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it wipes out her technician plan and she'd have to start over with about four months of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A basic safety net while people adjust, and simple ways for ordinary people to own a share of what the robots make.
